opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really important question, and I think it's one where the field is still figuring things out. My starting point is that these are genuinely different measurement questions. When you evaluate a component in isolation, like a retriever, a code interpreter, a calculator, or a particular prompt-and-model pairing, you're asking whether that piece does its job well under some distribution of inputs. When you evaluate the full system, you're asking whether the whole pipeline produces outcomes people actually care about. Those two things don't always line up the way you'd hope.

Part of the reason is that errors compose in non-obvious ways. A retriever might look mediocre on a standard retrieval benchmark, but if the downstream model is good at ignoring irrelevant context, the system might be fine. Or the opposite: every component looks great individually, but small errors compound across steps, or the model calls a tool at the wrong time or misreads its output. So component-level metrics are necessary, but they're not sufficient for predicting system behavior.

I think about it a bit like measurement in other engineering disciplines. You want unit tests and integration tests, and they serve different purposes. Component evaluations are great for diagnosis. When the system fails, you want to be able to localize the failure: was it retrieval, reasoning, tool selection, or how the output got formatted? Without component-level instrumentation you're left staring at an end-to-end number that went down, with no idea why.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that the input distribution a tool sees inside a system is often quite different from the distribution it was benchmarked on. The queries a language model sends to a search tool aren't the queries a human would type. So if you evaluate the tool in isolation on human-written queries, you might be measuring the wrong thing. One practical approach is to log the actual intermediate inputs from the running system and build component evaluations from those, so the isolated test reflects the conditions the component actually faces.

And then there's validity, which I care a lot about. You have to be clear about what construct you're trying to measure. If a component metric is a proxy for system quality, you should check empirically whether improving it actually moves the system-level outcome. Sometimes it does, and sometimes you're optimizing a number that doesn't matter.

So my short answer is to do both, but be deliberate. Use component evaluations for diagnosis and iteration, use system evaluations for the claims you ultimately want to make, and spend some effort understanding how the two relate rather than assuming one implies the other.

r002.rationale: It recommends checking whether component metrics track system outcomes, but does not mention embedding quality or its relationship to RAG performance in practice.

r003.rationale: The response says component errors can compose in non-obvious ways and that individually strong components may still produce failures through interactions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something I think about a lot, because the way we evaluate these systems hasn't really caught up with the way we're building them. A year or two ago, the unit of evaluation was the model. You had a benchmark, you ran the model, you got a number. Now the thing people actually deploy is a system: a model, a retriever, a set of tools it can call, maybe a planner on top, maybe some verification step. And the question of what you evaluate becomes much less obvious.

My instinct is that you need both levels, and they answer different questions. Evaluating a tool in isolation is really about reliability and specification. Does the retriever return relevant documents? Does the calculator or the code executor do what it says? Those are often well-posed problems with clear ground truth, and you can test them exhaustively in a way you simply can't test the full system. If a component is broken, you want to know that directly rather than inferring it from some end-to-end failure that could have five different causes.

But component evaluation has a real blind spot, which is that it assumes the interfaces are clean. In practice, the interesting failures live at the boundaries. The retriever returns something that's technically relevant, but the model misreads it. The tool returns a correct result, but the model decides not to call it, or calls it with the wrong arguments, or ignores the output and hallucinates anyway. None of that shows up if you test the tool by itself. So the full-system evaluation is where you find out whether the components compose, and composition is not something you get for free.

The analogy I keep coming back to is unit tests versus integration tests in software. Nobody thinks one replaces the other. What's different here, and I think harder, is that the "glue" between components is itself a stochastic model making judgment calls. So the integration failures aren't deterministic bugs, they're distributions over behaviors, and you need to think about them statistically. That's where a lot of my group's work has gone, on how you get reliable estimates and confidence intervals when every piece of the pipeline is noisy.

The other thing I'd flag is attribution. When the system fails, you want to know which component to blame, and naive end-to-end evaluation doesn't give you that. So one practical thing we recommend is to evaluate with interventions: swap in an oracle retriever, or an oracle tool, and see how much the end-to-end metric moves. That tells you where the headroom is and where the bottleneck is, and it's a lot more actionable than a single aggregate score.

So short version: evaluate tools separately to know they work, evaluate the system to know they work together, and use the gap between the two to figure out where the actual problem is.

r001.rationale: The response says separate evaluation helps establish reliability and identify broken components, but it does not say this enables tools to be mixed and matched.

r002.rationale: It discusses retriever relevance and system performance, but does not suggest that embedding-quality evaluations should correlate with a RAG tool’s practical performance.

r003.rationale: It explains that model decisions at component boundaries—such as failing to call a correct tool or ignoring its output—can cause failures that isolated tool evaluations do not reveal.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two distinct questions. One is, does the tool do what it’s supposed to do? And the other is, does the system know how to use it? You can have a very good tool, but if the model calls it at the wrong time, gives it the wrong inputs, or misinterprets the output, the overall system can still fail.

So I’d evaluate the tool in isolation, with a clear definition of its inputs and expected behavior. But then I’d also evaluate it in the context of the inputs it actually receives from the model. Those might look quite different from the clean examples you used to test the tool.

And ultimately, you need an end-to-end evaluation: did the system accomplish the user’s task? The component evaluations help you diagnose why it succeeded or failed. They don’t, by themselves, establish that the whole system works. That’s the distinction I’d keep coming back to.

r001.rationale: The response recommends separate tool evaluation but does not say this enables tools to be mixed and matched.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss embedding quality, RAG performance, or a correlation between them.

r003.rationale: It explains that a tool can pass isolated testing yet fail when the model calls it at the wrong time, supplies different inputs, or misinterprets its output.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you want to do both, because they answer different questions. When you evaluate a tool in isolation, you’re asking: given the right input, does this component do what we expect? If it’s a retrieval tool, does it return the relevant information? If it’s a calculator, does it execute the computation correctly?

But that doesn’t tell you whether the language model knows when to use the tool, how to formulate the input, or how to interpret the result. You can have a very good tool and still have a system that performs poorly because the model calls it at the wrong time or ignores what comes back.

So I’d look at component evaluations as a way to understand and diagnose the system, and then evaluate the full system on the task you actually care about. And when something fails, you want enough visibility into that interaction to distinguish a tool failure from a failure in how the model used it.

r002.rationale: It discusses retrieval returning relevant information, but makes no claim that embedding-quality evaluations correlate with a RAG tool’s practical performance.

r003.rationale: It explains that a good tool can still perform poorly in the full system because the model may call it at the wrong time, formulate inputs poorly, or ignore its results.
